body.text: For Canadian businesses considering a pre-claim consultation (PCC) on SR&ED eligibility, the CRA’s optional Pre-Claim Approval Process, launched April 1, 2026, lets claimants apply via My Business Account using Form T1322 before starting R&D work. Determinations typically arrive within eight weeks and can cover up to three years, but Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 must still be filed annually.

Canada's research and development (R&D) tax incentive framework—anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program—represents one of the most comprehensive volume-based fiscal support systems in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), delivering approximately 84% of federal R&D business support through indirect tax credits. Administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the Department of Finance Canada under the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945), the federal program operates through a dual-pillar statutory mechanism. First, subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act permits taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to pool eligible current and—for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024—capital SR&ED expenditures for an immediate 100% income deduction or an indefinite carryforward. Second, subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1), alongside section 127.1, generate Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) ranging from a basic rate of 15% to an enhanced refundable rate of 35%.

Between December 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian R&D tax regime underwent its most significant legislative expansion in over a decade. Following initial policy proposals in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (which proposed raising the enhanced expenditure limit to $4.5 million) and further enhancements in Budget 2025, Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $6 million (increasing the maximum annual refundable federal credit from $1.05 million to $2.1 million), raised the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the legacy $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million, extended the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) based on a three-year average revenue phase-out ($15 million to $75 million), allowed Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) to elect into the revenue-based phase-out regime, and restored the SR&ED eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched a formal, optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (utilizing Form T1322 and updated Form T661 Version 26) to provide upfront technical eligibility certainty prior to expenditure incurrence.

At the sub-national level, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits layer onto the federal framework, though provincial alignment with the 2025–2026 federal reforms varies markedly across jurisdictions. British Columbia expressly harmonized its 10% SR&ED tax credit with the federal $6 million expenditure limit, ECPC eligibility, $15 million–$75 million taxable capital phase-out, and restored capital expenditure base, while making its credit permanent in B.C. Budget 2026. Conversely, Quebec enacted a sweeping structural overhaul in its 2025–2026 Budget, replacing eight legacy innovation tax measures with the unified, 100% refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, offering 30% on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold and 20% thereafter. Ontario (8% refundable OITC up to $3 million; 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC; 20% refundable OBRITC up to $20 million) and Alberta (8% base and 20% incremental refundable Innovation Employment Grant up to $4 million) maintained their independent statutory caps and phase-out parameters. Because provincial R&D tax credits and direct grants such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act, they grind down the federal qualified expenditure pool—requiring precise multi-jurisdictional modelling to calculate net effective combined recovery rates.
1. Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Legislative History and Evolution of the Statutory Definition

Canada's statutory commitment to incentivizing industrial research through the tax system began in 1944, when the federal government amended the income tax legislation to permit companies to immediately deduct from their taxable income an amount equivalent to 100% of current expenditures related to scientific research. In 1963, the government promulgated section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations to establish the first formal regulatory definition of "scientific research," framing it as a systematic investigation or search carried out in the field of science by means of experimentation or analysis to acquire new knowledge, devise and develop new products or processes, or apply newly acquired knowledge to make improvements to existing products or processes. While the 1963 regulation explicitly included the development, testing, and evaluation of a prototype, it established foundational exclusions for market research, sales promotion, quality control, routine product testing, social sciences research, mineral or petroleum prospecting, explorations, or drilling (including geological and geophysical studies), preparation of facilities construction specifications, and operational instruction preparation prior to commercial production.

In 1967, section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations was amended to structure eligible work into three explicit categories—basic research, applied research, and development—while introducing five categories of eligible support activities (engineering or design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, and psychological research) and adding humanities research, commercial production or commercial use of a new or improved process, style changes, and routine data collection to the excluded categories. Following the 1970s tax reform, which renumbered the statutory deduction provision from section 72 to section 37 of the Income Tax Act (placing the definition reference in paragraph 37(7)(b), and adding a cross-reference to paragraph 37.1(5)(e) in 1978), taxpayers and practitioners increasingly found the administrative guidance in Interpretation Bulletin IT-439 insufficient to distinguish qualifying technological development from routine industrial engineering.

To resolve this ambiguity, the Department of Finance announced in its May 1985 Budget Papers that the regulatory definition would be amended to include the term "experimental development," confirming that projects involving only routine engineering or routine development were excluded. In 1986, the title "Scientific Research and Experimental Development" (SR&ED) was formally introduced into section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations (renumbered as subsection 2900(1) effective May 23, 1985). On March 4, 1986, in response to Revenue Canada's request for clarification, the Department of Finance confirmed three overarching principles: to qualify, an activity must embody scientific or technological advancement, contain scientific or technological uncertainty, and be conducted in a systematic and organized fashion to advance the understanding of scientific or technological relationships. Revenue Canada and industry leaders codified these principles in Information Circular IC 86-4 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development) in 1986, clarifying in 1992 that experimental development must seek technological advancement to create or improve materials, devices, products, or processes, and culminating in the landmark revision IC 86-4R3 in 1994.

Subsequent legislative amendments refined the statutory text into its modern structure. In 1994, the French version of the Regulations was updated to replace "recherches scientifiques et développement experimental" with "activités de recherche scientifique et de développement expérimental". In 1995 (applicable to taxation years ending after December 2, 1992), subsection 2900(1) was amended to update statutory references to sections 37 and 37.1 of the Income Tax Act, replace "development" in paragraph (c) with "experimental development" (explicitly including incremental improvements), group support work under paragraph (d) subject to a dual test requiring work to be both "commensurate with the needs" and "directly in support" of core research or experimental development, and expand support work to eight specific categories by adding data collection and testing.

In 1996, the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" was added to subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act for work performed after February 27, 1995, initially cross-referencing the meaning assigned by the regulation. In 1998, Parliament transferred the full substantive definition of SR&ED directly from Regulation 2900(1) into subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, replacing the conjunction "or" between paragraphs (c) and (d) with "and, in applying this definition in respect of a taxpayer, includes" and adding the requirement in paragraph (d) that support work be "undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer". Subsection 2900(1) of the Regulations was subsequently repealed on July 27, 2000 (applicable to 1995 and subsequent taxation years). On June 26, 2013, legislative amendments received Royal Assent to replace the French phrase "travaux techniques" in paragraph (d) with "travaux de génie" to maintain consistency with the English term "engineering". Administratively, the CRA published the consolidated Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy in 2012 (revised April 24, 2015 to replace references to "scientific method" with "systematic investigation or search" and "technology base or level" with "scientific or technological knowledge base"), before archiving that policy in August 2021 and replacing it with the current Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives.

body.text: 1.3 Detailed Analysis of Subsection 248(1): Eligible Work, Support Work, and Exclusions

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "scientific research and experimental development" is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". To qualify, the work must fall into one of three core categories in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c), or constitute eligible support work under paragraph (d), and must not fall within the statutory exclusions listed in paragraphs (e) through (k).

Under paragraph 248(1)(a), basic research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph 248(1)(b), applied research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, such as studying a newly discovered virus by exploiting identified characteristics of that virus. Under paragraph 248(1)(c), experimental development encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development is the most commonly claimed category in Canadian industrial claims. Crucially, the statutory inclusion of "incremental improvements thereto" confirms that a project does not need to create a revolutionary breakthrough; slight or gradual advances in the underlying technological knowledge base qualify provided they seek to resolve genuine technological uncertainty.

Under paragraph 248(1)(d), support work consists of work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive categories—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where that work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of core basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work cannot qualify on a standalone basis; if no core basic research, applied research, or experimental development exists in Canada, any standalone engineering, coding, or testing fails the statutory definition of SR&ED.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude seven categories of activity from the definition of SR&ED: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; and (k) routine data collection. As established in the CRA's administrative guidelines, the presence of an excluded activity within a broader company undertaking (such as mineral prospecting or commercial manufacturing) does not automatically disqualify the entire project. Rather, the exclusions are evaluated only after core SR&ED is established in order to draw the boundaries between eligible SR&ED work and non-SR&ED commercial activities. The fundamental criterion distinguishing eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as data collection or testing) from excluded work under paragraphs (f) or (k) (routine testing or routine data collection) is purpose: if the testing or data collection is carried out specifically to directly support an active SR&ED investigation, it qualifies as eligible support work; if it is performed routinely to support standard business operations such as quality assurance, it is excluded.
1.4 The CRA's "Why" and "How" Framework vs. The Five Questions

In August 2021, the CRA replaced the archived Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (which framed technical eligibility around the five questions derived from Northwest Hydraulic Consultants) with the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives. The current guidelines organize the statutory requirements of subsection 248(1) into two mandatory requirements that must both be satisfied for work to qualify.

First, under the "Why" Requirement, the work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement. The CRA emphasizes that qualifying work must focus on generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (such as theories or prediction models) that advances the understanding of science or technology, rather than merely gathering factual knowledge (such as data or measurements). The need for new scientific or technological knowledge arises only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists—meaning that whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, is unknown or uncertain due to an insufficiency in available scientific or technological knowledge (combining internal company knowledge and publicly available knowledge). Indicators of insufficient technological knowledge include situations where existing design methods are not applicable, requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards, too many variables or unknowns are present, parameters or conditions lie outside normal operating ranges, the nature of the problem is evolving, data is not readily available, or interlocking constraints exist. Attempting to resolve a recognized scientific or technological uncertainty constitutes an attempt to achieve scientific or technological advancement. If an uncertainty is circumvented using standard available knowledge or workarounds, the work is not eligible. Conversely, whether the project succeeds or fails in meeting its commercial or technical objectives does not affect eligibility; rejecting a hypothesis through testing still advances knowledge.

Second, under the "How" Requirement, the work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Simply following standard business design methods, standard procedures, or carrying out work systematically is not sufficient. Under the CRA guidelines, a valid systematic investigation or search comprises four necessary elements: (1) hypothesis or idea generation, which entails formulating an idea, proposed solution, proposed method, or approach consistent with known facts as a starting point for further investigation; (2) experimentation or analysis, which entails testing the hypothesis or idea through experiment or analysis while allowing the hypothesis to evolve based on results; (3) logical conclusions, which entails developing logical conclusions based on findings or experimental results; and (4) evidence collection, which entails keeping evidence that is generated as the work progresses. As the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72), the "Why" and "How" framework does not represent a departure from the five-part common-law test in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants: the first Northwest Hydraulic element (technical risk or uncertainty) is contained within the "Why" requirement, while the last four elements are rewritten and summarized within the "How" requirement.
1.5 Project Delineation and Shop-Floor SR&ED Boundaries

Under the CRA's guidelines, claimants must distinguish between a broad company project—which refers to commercial undertakings aimed at impacting a business, such as constructing or expanding facilities, developing product lines, or upgrading processes—and an SR&ED project, which refers specifically to a set of interrelated activities that are collectively necessary to attempt to achieve a specific scientific or technological advancement by overcoming scientific or technological uncertainty. An SR&ED project typically exists as a subset of a broader company project, and a single company project may contain one or multiple SR&ED projects.

An SR&ED project begins when scientific or technological uncertainties are identified and scientific or technological objectives are established. A technical feasibility study is eligible only if it is followed up with experimentation or analysis to test a hypothesis, whereas commercial, financial, or marketing studies are never eligible. Project duration does not determine eligibility; a project can take place within a single taxation year or span multiple taxation years. An SR&ED project ends when the uncertainty is resolved and advancement is achieved, or when it is determined that the uncertainty cannot be resolved. Financial milestones (such as a first sale), issuing warranties, commercialization, or certification do not automatically signal the end of an SR&ED project. However, post-development troubleshooting, debugging, fine-tuning where no technological uncertainties remain, and customer-site testing or beta testing to verify customer specifications are not SR&ED work unless a new technological uncertainty arises requiring systematic investigation. When experimental development occurs in production or manufacturing environments concurrently with commercial work ("shop-floor SR&ED"), claimants must apply the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy and the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy to isolate eligible experimental work from excluded commercial production.
2. Federal Deduction Pool (Section 37) and Investment Tax Credit Mechanics (Sections 127 & 127.1)
2.1 The Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act establishes a cumulative, running expenditure pool—calculated in Section C of Part 3 of Form T661—for taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada. Claimants may choose to deduct the entire positive balance available in the pool for the taxation year or any portion of it against business income, and any unclaimed balance carries forward indefinitely to reduce business income in future taxation years. Because the CRA treats the Section 37 pool as a continuous running balance, the specific taxation year to which individual expenditures relate is neither tracked nor required once the expenditures are validly identified on time on Form T661.

Pursuant to subsection 37(1) and the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, the pool balance is increased each taxation year by six statutory additions. First, under paragraph 37(1)(a), the pool increases by expenditures of a current nature incurred in the year on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i) and (i.01)) or qualifying third-party payments made to Canadian corporations and approved entities (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii)). Current expenditures include the SR&ED portion of salaries and wages (including up to 10% permissible foreign support wages under subsection 37(1.4)), the cost of materials consumed or transformed in SR&ED, equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant, third-party payments, and—when the Traditional Method is used—directly related and incremental overhead expenditures. (When the Proxy Method is elected, neither the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount [PPA] nor the actual overhead expenditures it represents are included in the Section 37 pool; actual overhead costs remain deductible as ordinary business expenses in the year.) Second, under paragraph 37(1)(b) (restored by Bill C-15), the pool increases by expenditures of a capital nature made for depreciable property acquired and available for use on or after December 16, 2024, intended to be used all or substantially all (90% or more) in SR&ED in Canada. Under amended subsection 37(6), amounts deducted under subsection 37(1) for capital property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 are treated as capital cost allowance (CCA) allowed to the taxpayer. Third, under paragraph 37(1)(c), the pool increases by repayments of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool. Fourth, under paragraph 37(1)(c.1), the pool increases by amounts included in income in the preceding taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(v). Fifth, under paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and (c.3), the pool increases by any SR&ED ITC recaptured in the prior taxation year or partnership ITC recapture excess amounts. Sixth, the pool increases by balances transferred upon an amalgamation or wind-up.

Conversely, the Section 37 pool is reduced each taxation year by six statutory deductions. First, under paragraph 37(1)(d), the pool is reduced by all government assistance (including provincial/territorial R&D tax credits and direct grants such as NRC IRAP) and non-government assistance that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date in respect of SR&ED expenditures included in the pool (including paragraph 37(1)(b) capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024). Assistance reduces SR&ED expenditures strictly on a project-by-project basis down to nil. Crucially, under the Proxy Method, the portion of a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit that relates to the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) does not reduce the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(d) because the PPA is not included in the pool; instead, that portion of the provincial credit must be included directly in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year received. Second, under paragraph 37(1)(d.1), the pool is reduced by any provincial "super-allowance benefit amount". Third, under paragraph 37(1)(e), the pool is reduced by all federal SR&ED ITCs deducted against Part I tax under subsection 127(5) or refunded in cash under section 127.1 in a preceding taxation year—including the portion of the federal ITC attributable to the PPA. (If reductions cause a negative pool balance, the negative amount is included in income under paragraph 12(1)(v).) Fourth, under paragraph 37(1)(f), the pool is reduced by amounts deducted under subsection 37(1) in preceding taxation years. Fifth, under paragraph 37(1)(f.1), the pool is reduced by insolvency deductions under section 61.39.

Sixth, under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1), upon a loss restriction event (an acquisition of control of a corporation or a change in majority-interest beneficiary of a trust), there is a deemed taxation year-end immediately before the event and the Section 37 pool is automatically reduced to nil. The undeducted pre-acquisition pool balance may be reinstated and deducted in a subsequent taxation year only if the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and the deduction is limited to the claimant's income for that year (before making any pool deduction) derived from that same business or a similar business. Finally, with respect to entity structure, a partnership is not permitted to carry forward any amount in its Section 37 pool to a subsequent fiscal period; the full pool balance at the end of the partnership's fiscal period must be deducted when computing partnership net income for that year.
2.2 Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Thresholds, and Bill C-15 Reforms

Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers earn SR&ED Investment Tax Credits as a specified percentage of their annual SR&ED qualified expenditure pool. Unlike the cumulative Section 37 deduction pool, the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool is calculated at the end of each taxation year on Part 4 of Form T661 and does not carry over to another taxation year.

Pursuant to paragraph 127(9)(a.1), the basic ITC rate is 15% of the taxpayer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year (less any provincial super-allowance benefit amount). This 15% basic rate applies to corporations that do not qualify for the enhanced rate (such as foreign-controlled corporations and non-qualifying public corporations), to individuals (sole proprietorships), to partners of a partnership, to beneficiaries of trusts, and to qualified expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their annual expenditure limit. Pursuant to subsection 127(10.1), an enhanced 20% ITC is added to the 15% basic rate—resulting in a total enhanced ITC rate of 35%—on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's annual expenditure limit.

Enacted on March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) substantially expanded the enhanced 35% ITC regime for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. body.text: Under subsection 127(10.2) of the Income Tax Act, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC's maximum $6,000,000 expenditure limit decreases gradually once its (or its associated corporate group's) taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year reaches $15,000,000, becoming nil once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000. However, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, subsections 127(10.31) (for a single CCPC) and 127(10.32) (for a CCPC with associated corporations, requiring a joint election by all CCPCs in the group) allow CCPCs to elect on a prescribed form to determine their expenditure limit using the revenue method—the same calculation used by Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) under subsection 127(10.6)—instead of relying on taxable capital. Under the revenue method, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit phases out based on the corporation's (or group's) average annual revenue over the preceding 3 fiscal years, beginning to decrease when 3-year average annual revenue reaches $15,000,000 and becoming nil at $75,000,000 or greater. For an associated CCPC group electing under subsection 127(10.32), the calculation aggregates the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of all group members for the preceding 3 fiscal years (including a reasonable share of revenue from partnerships or trusts, with reasonable adjustments allowed for intra-group sales of goods or services).

For Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—defined in subsection 127(9) to include qualifying public corporations resident in Canada and their eligible subsidiaries resident in Canada of which not less than 90% of the issued shares of each class of capital stock is owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more qualifying ECPCs—the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is shared among members of a consolidated group that prepare consolidated financial statements (defined in subsections 127(9) and 233.8(1) as financial statements in which the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of the group members are presented as those of a single economic entity). Associated CCPCs allocate their shared expenditure limit using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsection 127(10.3), while consolidated ECPCs allocate their shared limit under subsections 127(10.61) and 127(10.62). If an associated CCPC group or consolidated ECPC group fails to file an allocation agreement within 30 days after the Minister of National Revenue requests it, the Minister allocates the expenditure limit among the group under subsection 127(10.4) (for CCPCs) or subsection 127(10.63) (for ECPCs). For taxation years of less than 51 weeks, subsection 127(10.5) prorates the expenditure limit based on the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365.
2.3 Refundability Matrix and Carryover Rules (Section 127.1 & Subsection 127(5))

Earned SR&ED ITCs must first be applied against federal Part I tax otherwise payable in the current taxation year under subsection 127(5). Where no Part I tax is otherwise payable (or an unclaimed current-year ITC balance remains), section 127.1 (specifically subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), and 127.1(2.01)) governs the cash refundability of the unused credits. Under subsection 127.1(3), any SR&ED ITC refunded in the taxation year is deemed to have been applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable under subsection 127(5), which reduces the ITCs available for carryforward or carryback and reduces the following year's Section 37 deductible pool under paragraph 37(1)(e).

body.text: Any unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs remaining at the end of a taxation year may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (capped at the lesser of the current year's unused ITC after any refund and the prior year's Part I tax payable in excess of prior-year ITCs) or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce federal Part I tax payable. An acquisition of control restricts the carryforward of unused ITCs earned prior to the acquisition of control, as well as the carryback of unused ITCs earned after the acquisition of control. Furthermore, no amount is considered an ITC in respect of an SR&ED expenditure made in the course of earning income that is exempt from Part I tax (such as non-prescribed Crown corporations).
3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Proxy vs. Traditional Method, and Cost Category Rules
3.1 The Traditional Method vs. The Proxy Method (Subsection 37(8) & Regulation 2900)

Under subsections 37(8) and 37(10) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must choose between two statutory methods for computing its SR&ED expenditures and overhead for each taxation year: the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)) or the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)). The election is made in Section A of Part 3 of Form T661 by ticking Line 160 for the Proxy Method (and completing Part 5) or Line 162 for the Traditional Method (entering "0" on Lines 355 and 502 and skipping Part 5). Pursuant to subsection 37(10), the election must be made on the day the claimant first files Form T661 for the taxation year; if no election is selected, the Traditional Method applies by default. Once Form T661 is filed for a specific taxation year, the choice between the Traditional and Proxy methods is locked (irrevocable) for that taxation year, though the claimant may switch methods in subsequent taxation years.

body.text: When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations sets the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) at 55% of the eligible salary base (reduced from 65% for 2012 and prior years and 60% for 2013). Consequently, the Proxy Method yields a larger Investment Tax Credit than the Traditional Method whenever provable, directly related, and incremental SR&ED overhead is less than 55% of the eligible salary base. However, constructing the salary base in Section A of Part 5 of Form T661 is subject to three strict regulatory constraints under section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations.

First, under subsection 2900(9), for every employee (whether arm's length or a specified employee), the salary base must exclude four categories of remuneration: (1) taxable benefits under sections 6 and 7 of the Income Tax Act; (2) unpaid amounts from a prior taxation year that were disallowed under subsection 78(4) and paid in the current taxation year (reported on Line 310 of Form T661); (3) remuneration based on profits; and (4) bonuses. Employer contributions to related benefit plans are also excluded from the salary base. Second, under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8), the amount included in the salary base for a specified employee is capped at the lesser of 75% of total eligible salary or wages and 2.5 × YMPE prorated by days employed in the year (shared across associated corporations). Third, under subsection 2900(6), in Section B of Part 5 of Form T661, the calculated 55% PPA cannot exceed the Overall Cap on the PPA, calculated using the formula A - B - C. In this formula, A is the total amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from all businesses carried on by the claimant for the year (including cost of goods sold); B is the sum of deductions claimed for the year under sections 20 (e.g., CCA, interest, bad debts), 24 (ceasing to carry on a business), 26 (banks), 30 (improving land for farming), 32 (insurance agents/brokers), 37 (SR&ED expenditures), 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and 104 (trusts); and C is the amount of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building.
3.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, and Foreign Support Work

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, "salary or wages" is defined in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act as income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I (sections 5 to 8). This includes regular wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, honorariums, director or management fees, commissions, cash outlays for taxable benefits, and reasonable estimates of actual costs incurred for non-cash taxable benefits (such as automobile standby charges, excluding GST/HST or PST where an input tax credit is claimed, provided the actual costs are not already claimed as a standard business expense). Conversely, dividends paid to shareholders are a return on shares rather than income from employment; therefore, dividends never qualify as SR&ED salary or wages or enter the PPA salary base. Extended vacation or sick leave (beyond normal accrual), employee stock option benefits, and retiring allowances are also excluded from SR&ED salary or wages.

Under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV)), allowable salaries are restricted to employees "directly engaged" in SR&ED—meaning hands-on work encompassed by paragraphs 248(1)(a) to (d). Whether an employee is directly engaged is determined by the tasks performed rather than the employee's job title. Managers and supervisors qualify only when directing the technical course of ongoing SR&ED work or providing direct technical input; non-technological management or decision-making functions do not qualify, and work beyond first-line supervision rarely qualifies. Under the Traditional Method, in addition to employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support SR&ED, a claimant may claim on Line 360 the administrative salaries of clerical, human resources, accounting, and purchasing staff providing services to SR&ED employees, provided those duties are non-technological, directly related (with no intervening step), and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, a "specified employee" is an employee who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time in the taxation year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or a related corporation (a specified shareholder), or who does not deal at arm's length with the corporation (such as a spouse, sibling, or other related family member of a controlling shareholder, even if that family member holds no shares). For the 10% share ownership test, shares owned by persons with whom the employee does not deal at arm's length are included, shares held through a partnership or fixed trust count proportionately, and a beneficiary of a discretionary family trust is treated as owning 100% of the trust's shares. Ownership at any time during the taxation year classifies the individual as a specified employee for that year.

Being classified as a specified employee triggers three strict statutory restrictions. First, under subsection 37(9), any remuneration based on profits or a bonus paid or payable to a specified employee is completely excluded from SR&ED expenditures under both the Traditional and Proxy methods (whereas bonuses and profit-based pay for non-specified employees are allowable direct SR&ED wages, though excluded from the PPA salary base under Reg 2900(9)). Second, under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages claimable on Line 305 (and Line 309) for a specified employee under both the Traditional and Proxy methods is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual is a specified employee. Under subsections 37(9.2) to 37(9.4), if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, this single 5 × YMPE cap is shared across the group via prescribed Form T1174; if the associated corporations fail to file the agreement, none of the specified employee's salary is allowable in any of the associated corporations. Third, under Regulation 2900(7), the amount included in the Part 5 PPA salary base for a specified employee is restricted to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages) and 2.5 × YMPE prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year (2.5 × YMPE × [Days Employed ÷ 365]), with a single 2.5 × YMPE ceiling shared across associated corporations under Regulation 2900(8).

With respect to work performed outside Canada, under subsection 37(1.4) of the Income Tax Act and section 10.0 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, permissible salary or wages paid to employees carrying on SR&ED work outside Canada may be claimed on Line 307 (for employees other than specified employees) and Line 309 (for specified employees) of Form T661, provided that the foreign work is performed "solely in support" of SR&ED carried on by the claimant in Canada and the salary or wages are not subject to an income or profits tax from another country. Finally, two 180-day unpaid expenditure rules apply to SR&ED claims. Under subsection 78(4), any salary or wages incurred in the taxation year that are not paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year; they must be identified on Line 315 of Form T661 and can only be claimed on Line 310 in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (and Line 310 amounts are excluded from the PPA salary base under Regulation 2900(9)). Similarly, under the Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, any current SR&ED expenditures other than salary or wages (such as subcontractor or material invoices) that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are excluded from qualified expenditures for ITC purposes in that year and are added back to become qualified expenditures in the subsequent taxation year in which they are paid (at 80% for arm's-length contracts or third-party payments).
3.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Regulation 2900(2)(a))

Under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II) of the Income Tax Act, paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Income Tax Regulations, and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, a claimant may claim the cost of "materials consumed" (Form T661 Line 320) or "materials transformed" (Form T661 Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

To constitute "materials for SR&ED," the raw materials, substances, or other items must be physical and tangible (generally in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) and must, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, compose the body of a tangible object ("a thing") on which the SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED being carried out. If the claimant is developing or improving a process, items qualify as materials only if they compose the body of a tangible object involved in testing the new or improved process. For purchased items (which may be acquired from Canadian or foreign suppliers), cost means the laid-down cost, including invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, acquisition, storage, and external processing services (such as contracted galvanization of metal parts prior to SR&ED testing). For self-manufactured goods or inventory drawn into SR&ED, cost includes production cost or industrial cost price under generally accepted accounting principles (laid-down cost of materials, direct labour, and a share of production overhead—with production overhead included even when the claimant elects the Proxy Method). When materials are purchased from a non-arm's length party, the ITC earned is restricted to the cost incurred by the non-arm's length supplier (excluding any intercompany profit element).

Items that do not compose the body of the tangible experimental object—such as broken or used laboratory glassware (petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes), cleaning supplies, general utilities (water, electricity, oil, natural gas, propane, or boiler feed water used for steam/energy), CDs/DVDs, used lubricants/engine oil, software licences, and data purchases—do not qualify as materials for SR&ED on Lines 320 or 325. (Under the Traditional Method, laboratory supplies and variable utilities may qualify as overhead on Line 360 if directly related and incremental.) In agricultural or biological research, seeds, growth media, agar, fungal cultures, animal feed, fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides applied to experimental test plots or animals qualify as materials, whereas animals or plants in a control group (receiving no experimental treatment) do not qualify. Crucially, the cost of materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the materials are actually consumed or transformed in SR&ED, never when they are merely purchased and held in inventory.

The distinction between Line 320 and Line 325 turns on whether the materials retain value after testing. Materials Consumed (Line 320) are materials destroyed, absorbed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless—meaning 90% or more of their value/cost was consumed—as a result of the SR&ED (if experimental production is sold for more than 10% of its original cost, the materials are considered not to have been consumed). Materials Transformed (Line 325) are materials for SR&ED that have been transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED but retain more than 10% of their value (less than 90% consumed), such as components incorporated into a custom product, prototype, or commercial asset. Subsequent sale or conversion to commercial use of transformed materials (or animals/growing things) within 20 years triggers ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) to (36).
3.4 Subcontractor Expenditures and Third-Party Payments

Canadian tax law distinguishes sharply between SR&ED contracts (performed on behalf of the claimant under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and the Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy) and third-party payments (made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or corporations under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii) and the Third-Party Payments Policy). In an SR&ED contract, the work is controlled by the payer, intellectual property rights are exclusive to the payer, the contract is usually limited to one payer, the work has a commercial focus, and tax treatment is on an accrual basis (subject to the subsection 18(9) prepaid expense limitation for work not yet performed). In a third-party payment, the SR&ED work is controlled by the performer (such as a university or research institute that might have conducted the research anyway), rights are non-exclusive (generally published, though the payer must receive a preferential right to exploit the results), there is usually more than one funder, the work is often basic or applied research, and tax treatment is generally on a cash basis.

When a claimant enters into an arm's-length SR&ED contract for basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work carried on in Canada, 100% of the allowable contract cost enters the claimant's Section 37 deductible pool, while 80% of the expenditure enters the claimant's qualified expenditure pool for ITC calculation. To earn ITCs, the arm's-length contractor must be a "taxable supplier" under subsection 127(9)—defined as a person resident in Canada, a Canadian partnership, or a non-resident person/partnership receiving the amount in the course of carrying on business through a permanent establishment in Canada. For the arm's-length contractor (performer), the amount receivable from the payer constitutes a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(18), which reduces the performer's own qualified SR&ED expenditures to prevent double-dipping of ITCs. (Note that an arm's-length performer hired only to perform paragraph 248(1)(d) support work cannot claim SR&ED on its own tax return because support work on its own does not meet the definition of SR&ED, whereas the payer can claim the contract as support work tied to the payer's core SR&ED.) Contract costs for non-SR&ED trades (such as electricians, welders, or mechanics) do not qualify as SR&ED contracts, though they may qualify as overhead under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental.

Conversely, when a claimant enters into a non-arm's length (NAL) SR&ED contract, the payer's contract expenditure is an allowable deduction in the payer's Section 37 pool, but under paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), it is not a qualified expenditure and earns 0% ITCs for the payer. Instead, the payment is not treated as a contract payment to the NAL performer, and the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED expenditures (including standalone support work) to earn the ITC. Under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and payer may jointly execute Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer all or a portion of the performer's qualified expenditures to the payer (reported by the performer on Line 540 of Form T661). The transferable amount on Form T1146 is the least of: (1) the amount specified by the parties on Form T1146; (2) the performer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at year-end before the transfer (including its PPA); and (3) the hypothetical contract payment total paid by the payer within 180 days after the performer's year-end. If the performer attempts to transfer more than its qualified expenditure pool, the Income Tax Act dictates that no amount can be transferred. Partnerships cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures under Form T1146. Anti-avoidance rules also prevent a payer from interposing an arm's-length intermediary between itself and an NAL performer to circumvent these rules.

For third-party payments, eligible recipients (Entities A to F) include corporations resident in Canada (Entity A, claimable only in the year the SR&ED is performed), approved associations (Entity B), approved universities, colleges, and research institutes (Entity C—public Canadian universities and affiliated colleges are automatically approved, while other B and C entities require written ministerial approval through the Income Tax Rulings Directorate), tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under paragraph 149(1)(j) (Entity D), approved granting councils (Entity E), and pre-competitive basic/applied research consortia (Entity F). The claimant must be entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED in its business (either via rights to resulting patents/products or, for published academic research, via a preferential right such as early access to pre-publication prints before the results enter the public domain). Only 80% of a third-party payment qualifies for ITCs, payments to acquire or rent buildings are excluded, and the claimant must complete and attach Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment.
3.5 Overhead, Cloud Computing / SaaS Costs, and Prescribed Expenditures

Under the Traditional Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and subsections 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations), overhead and other expenditures claimed on Line 360 of Form T661 must satisfy two cumulative tests set out in the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy: (1) the Directly Related Test, requiring the expenditure to connect directly—without any intervening step or intermediary—to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED; and (2) the Incremental Test, requiring that the expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Fixed costs (such as a fixed annual equipment maintenance contract or standard monthly telephone, cellular, and internet service plans) fail the incremental test and are not allowable, whereas variable costs (such as metered electricity, gas, or water used to operate SR&ED equipment, dedicated long-distance charges, moving expenses to relocate SR&ED employees within Canada, reimbursed Canadian travel/lodging expenses to conduct experimental testing at a customer or supplier site, or a reasonable square-footage allocation of municipal taxes, building insurance, safety/security, and maintenance for a claimant-owned facility under subsection 2900(3)) qualify when supported by a reasonable allocation method. Pre-employment recruiting costs (headhunter fees, job advertising, interview travel, and immigration/visa costs) are disallowed. Under the Traditional Method, the employer's share of related benefits (CPP/QPP, EI, WSIB/CNESST, approved pension plans, medical/dental/optical insurance, supplementary sick benefits, and qualifying employer health tax contributions) is allowable on Line 360 only for direct SR&ED employees; related benefits, training, and travel for clerical or administrative support staff are disallowed as an indirect "overhead on overhead expenditure".

For software, artificial intelligence (AI), and Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) companies claiming cloud computing expenses (Amazon Web Services [AWS], Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform [GCP]), claimants must segregate cloud billing accounts or apply automated resource tags to separate production infrastructure (hosting customer-facing commercial applications, which belongs in Cost of Goods Sold [COGS]) and commercial third-party APIs from dedicated R&D development, experimental staging, or AI GPU training runs. Because software licences and cloud services are not physical solid, liquid, or gaseous objects composing the body of a tangible thing under the Materials for SR&ED Policy (despite loose descriptions in some startup marketing blogs), metered experimental cloud compute is claimed under the Traditional Method on Line 360 as directly related and incremental overhead, whereas under the Proxy Method general cloud hosting and software subscriptions are covered by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) unless a post-December 15, 2024 hardware server lease qualifies under the equipment lease rules on Line 350 or Line 355.

Pursuant to section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations and the Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, the following prescribed expenditures are excluded from earning SR&ED ITCs even if they are directly related and incremental: (1) legal or accounting fees—explicitly including third-party consulting or professional fees paid for preparing the technical or financial parts of an SR&ED claim (though internal salaries paid to regular employees for preparing SR&ED claims are allowed if directly related and incremental); (2) interest and financing costs under paragraphs 20(1)(c) to (g) of the Income Tax Act; (3) entertainment, advertising, or selling expenses; (4) convention or conference fees and expenses; (5) membership dues or fees in scientific or technical societies; and (6) fines or penalties.
3.6 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), Lease Costs, and Recapture

Effective for property acquired and lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 restored SR&ED tax incentives for capital property and leased equipment (which had been repealed between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024):

Under paragraph 37(1)(b) and the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy, SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Form T661 Line 390, Box 782) apply to depreciable property owned by the claimant that is acquired and available for use (under subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024, where at the time of acquisition the claimant intended that it would be used during all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada, or that 90% or more (ASA) of its value would be consumed in SR&ED in Canada. Capital cost includes the purchase price, installation costs, customs and excise duties, transportation, and other acquisition costs. Land, inventory, goodwill, and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings (paragraph 37(8)(e), except prescribed special-purpose buildings under Reg 2903) are excluded. Under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF—office desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, bookshelves, photocopiers, fax machines, telephones, cell phones, and calculators; note that computers, hardware, software, and ancillary equipment are NOT GPOEF) is excluded. While used or refurbished depreciable property meeting the 90% ASA test can be included in the Section 37 deductible pool on Line 390, it is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902 that must be deducted on Line 535 of Form T661 and cannot earn an ITC. Claimants must report the 10 most expensive SR&ED properties claimed on Line 390 and their SR&ED operating time percentages on Lines 262 and 263 of Form T661, and must not duplicate Line 390 property on Schedule T2SCH8 (CCA).

Under the SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, brand-new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA test, is not GPOEF, and is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under subsection 2900(11) of the Income Tax Regulations (equipment intended at acquisition to be used during commercial plant/line assembly or commissioning and primarily for commercial purposes over its useful life) qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE, Form T661 Line 504) if it is actually used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada. The capital cost of SUE does not enter the Section 37 pool (it is depreciated via regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8), but under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, 25% (1/4) of the capital cost (excluding borrowing costs and adjusted for NAL transfers under subsection 127(11.6)) qualifies for ITCs on Line 504 as First Term SUE at the end of the first taxation year occurring at least 12 months after acquisition, and an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost qualifies as Second Term SUE at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition. Any ITC earned on SUE and claimed or refunded reduces the undepreciated capital cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the subsequent year.

Under the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 (evaluated over the full taxation year, or over the post-December 15, 2024 period for straddle years) qualify as follows: under the Traditional Method, 100% is claimed on Line 350 if used >=90% (ASA) for SR&ED (including GPOEF), or a proportional percentage is claimed on Line 360 as overhead if used <90% and directly attributable. Under the Proxy Method (excluding GPOEF), 100% is claimed on Line 350 if used >=90% (ASA), 50% (1/2) of the lease cost is claimed on Line 355 if used primarily (>50% to <90% of operating time), and 0% is allowed if used <=50%. Building rent is always excluded (except prescribed special-purpose buildings under Reg 2903), whereas land lease costs may qualify as overhead under the Traditional Method only.

Finally, under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) and the Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant disposes of, or converts to commercial use, any property on which an SR&ED ITC was earned within the 20 preceding taxation years (including transformed materials incorporated into a custom product or commercial asset, ASA capital equipment, SUE, animals/growing things, or physical property acquired under an SR&ED contract, but excluding intellectual property that always belonged to the payer), the claimant must add recaptured ITCs directly to its Part I tax payable for the year. The recapture amount is the lesser of the historical ITC earned on the property and the historical ITC rate (e.g., 35%, 15%, or 20% pre-2014) applied to the proceeds of disposition (for an arm's-length sale) or the fair market value (FMV) (for conversion to commercial use or non-arm's length disposition)—with SUE recapture calculated on 25% or 50% of the proceeds/FMV. Under the CRA's de minimis rule, no recapture applies if proceeds or FMV are less than 10% of the property's original cost. Dispositions of ASA capital property to a non-arm's length purchaser that continues to use the property ASA for SR&ED defer recapture under subsections 127(33)–(35). Any recaptured ITC added to tax payable in a year is added back to increase the claimant's Section 37 deductible pool in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2).
4. Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Stacking Mechanics
4.1 Statutory Definitions and Accrual Recognition Rules

Under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, both the Section 37 deductible pool (via paragraph 37(1)(d)) and the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool (via subsections 127(18) to (20)) must be reduced by all government assistance (reported on Form T661 Line 514 for provincial/territorial assistance and Line 429 / 431) and non-government assistance (Line 432) that the claimant "has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive" on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year.

Government assistance is defined in subsection 127(9) as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (including Crown corporations, foreign governments, and non-profit organizations funded by government) whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax (including all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits), investment allowance, or any other form of assistance, other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself. Non-government assistance is defined as an amount that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) (read without reference to subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(v) to (vii)) as an inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance. Crucially, if a government funding agreement (such as a contribution from the Strategic Response Fund or a regional agency) stipulates that repayments depend on future project revenues or royalties, caps periodic repayments, or ends repayment obligations on a set date regardless of whether the full amount is repaid, the CRA classifies the contribution as a forgivable loan (government assistance) rather than an unconditional business loan. When repayments are subsequently made, they increase the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and earn ITCs in the year repaid.
4.2 Stacking Federal SR&ED with NRC IRAP Under the Proxy Method

For Canadian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs with 500 or fewer employees), the premier R&D funding strategy is stacking a non-repayable grant from the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) (median award ~$75,000, typical up to $1 million, up to $10 million ceiling for major projects) with the federal SR&ED tax credit under the Proxy Method. While an NRC IRAP salary reimbursement is government assistance that reduces the Section 37 pool (paragraph 37(1)(d)) and the qualified expenditure pool (subsection 127(18)), NRC IRAP assistance does NOT reduce the eligible direct SR&ED salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA).
Worked Calculation: Stacking NRC IRAP (80% Salary Coverage) + Federal SR&ED (Proxy Method)

Consider a qualifying CCPC (before provincial credits) that incurs $200,000 in direct, hands-on SR&ED salaries (non-specified employees) during its 2026 taxation year and receives an NRC IRAP grant reimbursing 80% ($160,000) of those salaries:

items: Direct SR&ED Salaries (Form T661 Line 300): $200,000.
Part 5 Eligible Salary Base for PPA: $200,000 (unreduced by the NRC IRAP grant).
Prescribed Proxy Amount (55% of $200,000 on Line 502): $110,000.
Gross Qualified Expenditures Before Assistance ($200,000 + $110,000): $310,000.
Less: Government Assistance (80% NRC IRAP Grant): -$160,000.
Net Federal SR&ED Qualified Expenditures: $150,000 (comprising the $40,000 remaining 20% salary portion that IRAP does not cover plus the full $110,000 PPA).
Federal Enhanced Refundable ITC (35% of $150,000): $52,500 cash refund.
Total Combined Non-Dilutive Cash Recovery ($160,000 IRAP + $52,500 SR&ED ITC): $212,500—representing 106.25% of the $200,000 direct R&D salary outlay.

body.text: 5.2 Deep-Dive into Major Provincial Jurisdictions and Combined Rate Math

In Quebec, the 2025–2026 Budget replaced eight separate innovation tax credits—including the legacy R&D wage credit (Form RD-1029.7), the university/public research contract credit (Form RD-1029.8.6), the private research partnership credit (Form RD-1029.8.16.1), the research consortium fees credit (Form RD-1029.8.9.03), and the foreign researcher tax holiday—with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. Claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR alongside Form RD-222 (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures) with the CO-17 return within 18 months of fiscal year-end, the CRIC is 100% refundable for all corporations regardless of size. It provides a 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures above an annual exclusion threshold (allocated across associated corporations on Line 160 of Form RD-1029.8.CR) and a 20% refundable credit on all excess eligible expenditures. The annual exclusion threshold is the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Quebec basic personal amounts ($18,571 in 2025; $18,952 in 2026) per R&D employee, prorated by R&D time. Crucially, CRIC expands eligibility beyond core R&D to include pre-commercialization activities connected to Quebec R&D (regulatory approval/certification testing, validation, product design, and certain quality control activities), covering 100% of salaries, 50% of subcontractor and university/public research institute payments, and 100% of new capital property. Only the R&D portion of the CRIC (Line 180 of Form RD-1029.8.CR) flows to Line 71 of Form RD-222 and Line 429a of federal Form T661 as government assistance. Operating alongside CRIC, Quebec's e-business tax credit (CDAE, Form CO-1029.8.36.DA, requiring Investissement Québec corporate and employee certificates within 15 months of year-end for IT firms with >=75% IT activities and >=6 technical staff working >=26 hours/week) offers a 30% credit (24% refundable + 6% non-refundable) up to $83,333 salary ($25,000 credit) per employee in 2025, before transitioning to the AI-focused CDAE-IA for taxation years starting after December 31, 2025.

In Ontario, three credits operate under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario). First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC, Section 96, Schedule T2SCH566) provides an 8% refundable credit on up to $3,000,000 of eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (maximum $240,000 per year, shared across an associated group), phasing out between $500,000 and $800,000 of prior-year associated taxable income OR between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year specified paid-up capital. Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC, Sections 38–45, Schedule T2SCH508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit (carryback 3 years, carryforward 20 years, reported on Schedule 5 Line 416) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures after first deducting the 8% OITC as government assistance. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC, Section 97, Schedules T2SCH568 & T2SCH569) provides a 20% refundable credit on qualified expenditures under eligible contracts with qualifying Ontario research institutes.
To illustrate the exact federal-provincial assistance grind in Ontario, when a qualifying CCPC incurs $1,000,000 of eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures:

items: Ontario OITC (Schedule 566): $1,000,000 × 8.0% = $80,000 (refundable).
Ontario ORDTC Base (Schedule 508): $1,000,000 - $80,000 (OITC) = $920,000.
Ontario ORDTC (Schedule 508): $920,000 × 3.5% = $32,200 (non-refundable; combined Ontario rate = 11.22%).
Federal Qualified Expenditure Base (Form T661 Line 514 grind): $1,000,000 - $80,000 - $32,200 = $887,800.
Federal Enhanced SR&ED ITC (Schedule 31): $887,800 × 35.0% = $310,730 (refundable).
Total Combined Federal + Ontario Tax Credits: $80,000 + $32,200 + $310,730 = $422,930, or 42.293% of eligible expenditures.
