6. Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, Deadlines, and Statutory Penalties
6.1 Prescribed Forms and the 2026 Form T661 Architecture

Under subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, accessing both SR&ED incentives requires submitting Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, or Form T2038(IND) for individuals and trusts) containing all prescribed information on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline. Depending on the claimant's circumstances, Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 are supplemented by Schedule T2SCH49 (associated CCPC expenditure limit allocation), Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), Form T1146 (NAL transfer of qualified expenditures), Form T1174 (associated corporation specified employee salary allocation), and Form T1263 (third-party payments).
In May 2026, the CRA released Form T661 Version 26 (t661-26e.pdf / t661-fill-26e.pdf, accompanied by Guide T4088) to implement the Bill C-15 reforms. Form T661 consists of ten parts:

items: Part 1 (General Information): Claimant identification, business number, and taxation year.

Part 2 (Project Information): Section A includes Line 207 (5-digit Statistics Canada CRDC 2020 Version 2.0 Field of Research code, entered as RDF followed by the five digits), Line 212 (Pre-claim approval checkbox), and Line 214 (Pre-claim approval case number). Section B captures the project technical narratives establishing the "Why" and "How" requirements (for classified projects designated for national security reasons by a federal agency, Section B is kept on a separate sheet in the claimant's records and a copy of the designation letter is filed with Form T661). Section C captures Lines 262 and 263 (names and SR&ED operating time percentages of the 10 most expensive depreciable SR&ED properties acquired after December 15, 2024 and claimed on Line 390), Line 265 (foreign support salary indicator), Line 266 (work carried out on behalf of another party), and the contemporaneous evidence checklist.

Part 3 (Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures): Section A records the irrevocable election between the Proxy Method (Line 160) and Traditional Method (Line 162); Section B computes allowable current expenditures (Line 380, including salaries on Lines 300, 305, 307, 309, 310, 315, materials consumed on Line 320, materials transformed on Line 325, ASA equipment leases on Line 350, Proxy primary equipment leases on Line 355, and Traditional overhead on Line 360), restored capital expenditures (Line 390, Box 782), and total allowable SR&ED expenditures (Line 400); Section C computes the Section 37 deductible pool (including assistance on Lines 429, 429a–e, 431, 432, other deductions/CCA recapture on Line 440, and the current-year deduction claimed on Line 455).

Part 4 (Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes): Computes total qualified SR&ED expenditures (Line 559) by adding the PPA (Line 502) and First/Second Term SUE (Line 504) and deducting provincial/territorial assistance (Line 514), federal/other assistance and contract payments (Line 513), 20% of arm's-length contracts and third-party payments, unpaid current costs at 180 days, prescribed expenditures including used capital property (Line 535), and NAL transfers (Line 540).
Part 5 (Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount): Section A computes the salary base and Section B computes the 55% PPA subject to the Overall PPA Cap.
Parts 6, 7, 8, and 10: Project-by-project cost allocation (Part 6), statistical data (Part 7), claim checklist (Part 8), and authorized officer certification (Part 10).

Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information): Mandatory disclosure of every claim preparer that accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim and their billing/contingency fee arrangements (if no external preparer assisted, complete only Lines 935, 970, and 975).

body.text: 6.2 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline (Subsections 37(11) & 37(12))

Under subsection 37(11) of the Income Tax Act and the SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, the SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, adding the 12-month statutory reporting window yields a strict corporate deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year (if the taxation year ends on the last day of a month, the deadline is the last day of the 18th month). For individuals (sole proprietors), the window is 17.5 months from the end of the taxation year.

Under subsection 37(12), no extensions are permitted. If Form T661 (containing the prescribed information in Parts 1–8 and 10) is not filed on or before the 18-month reporting deadline, the expenditures are statutorily deemed not to be SR&ED expenditures, and the claimant permanently forfeits both the Section 37 deduction and all ITCs. If Form T661 is filed on time by the 18-month deadline, but Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) is filed after the 18-month deadline, the allowable SR&ED expenditures can still be deducted or pooled under Section 37, but no ITC can be earned on those expenditures. (If prescribed SR&ED forms are filed on time without an income tax return, filing requirements are met, though processing is delayed until the tax return is filed.)
6.3 Statutory Penalties: Subsection 162(5.1) ($1,000 Penalty) and Subsection 163(2) / (2.21)

Unlike Parts 1–8 and 10, Part 9 of Form T661 (claim preparer information) is not subject to the 18-month disallowance rule; an SR&ED claim will never be disallowed solely because Part 9 information is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate. However, under subsections 162(5.1), 162(5.2), and 162(5.3) of the Income Tax Act, if the prescribed claim preparer and billing arrangement information in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty applies per claim, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable. Furthermore, overstated or false SR&ED claims are subject to gross negligence and false statement penalties under subsections 163(2) and 163(2.21) of the Income Tax Act.
7. CRA Audit and Review Process, Pre-Claim Approval, and Dispute Resolution
7.1 The 2026 Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Form T1322)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process enabling eligible businesses to obtain a formal technical eligibility determination before starting a proposed R&D project or incurring costs. Applications are submitted via My Business Account using Form T1322 (Application for SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval), and businesses may request one-on-one information sessions by emailing OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca. The CRA typically provides a determination within 8 weeks and can approve projects for a period of up to three years, subject to program conditions. Because pre-claim approval determines the eligibility of the proposed work rather than the final quantum of expenditures, claimants must still file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 annually, checking Line 212 and entering their pre-claim approval case number on Line 214 of Form T661.
7.2 Dual-Reviewer CRA Audit Architecture (RTA & FR) and the 13-Step Workflow

When a filed SR&ED claim is selected for review, it is examined jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA)—who evaluates whether the claimed projects satisfy the "Why" and "How" technical eligibility requirements and examines contemporaneous technical evidence—and a Financial Reviewer (FR)—who examines financial documentation, general ledgers, payroll, contracts, overhead allocations, and ITC calculations. Under the CRA's Financial Claim Review Manual, the coordinated review follows a 13-step sequence:

items: The FR receives the file from the control function.
The FR searches for and examines available information.
The FR contacts the RTA to initiate coordination.
Review planning begins by identifying issues and assessing risk and materiality.
The scope of the review is determined and a review plan is developed.
The reviewers determine who to contact for information.
The reviewers communicate with the claimant to gather additional information by letter, telephone, and/or visiting the claimant's premises.
The reviewers analyze the information and resolve issues.
The review plan is adjusted if required (returning to Step 7 if adjustments are made).
Addressing all technical and financial issues is completed.

The FR and RTA prepare a Proposal Letter Package (summarizing technical and financial findings, explaining any proposed adjustments, and enclosing a copy of the RTA's SR&ED Review Report) and provide the claimant with options for dispute resolution.
The FR and RTA consider written rebuttals and additional representations submitted by the claimant within the 30-day response window.
The FR issues the final letter and finalizes the Financial Review Report (FRR) and processing documents.

body.text: 7.3 Three-Tier Administrative Dispute Resolution and Formal Judicial Appeals

If a claimant disagrees with the findings of the RTA or FR during the review, the CRA's Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns (Application Policy SR&ED 2000-02R) establishes a three-step administrative dispute resolution process prior to assessment: first, speaking directly with the RTA or FR to resolve concerns; second, escalating to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) or Financial Review Manager (FRM); and third, requesting an Administrative Second Review. Once a formal Notice of (Re)assessment is issued, if the dispute remains unresolved, the claimant may file a formal Notice of Objection (NOO) with the Chief of Appeals at their local Tax Services Office (TSO), or appeal to the Tax Court of Canada (TCC), with further appeal to the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) and the Supreme Court of Canada (SCC).
8. Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents
8.1 Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC)

Authored by Judge Donald Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada), Northwest Hydraulic Consultants is the foundational judicial authority establishing the analytical framework for SR&ED eligibility in Canada. Justice Bowman set out the five-question common-law test—each of which must be answered in the affirmative for work to qualify:

items: Is there a technical risk or uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? "Routine engineering" describes techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field; if the resolution is reasonably predictable using standard procedures, no technological uncertainty exists, and the knowledge must actually be absent from the general scientific or technological knowledge base rather than merely unknown to the claimant.

Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? This entails a five-stage methodology: (a) observation of the subject matter of the problem; (b) formulation of a clear objective; (c) identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (d) formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (e) methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses.

Did the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? Intuitive creativity and genius can play a crucial role, provided they operate within the total discipline of the scientific method.

Did the process result in a technological advancement? Most scientific research involves gradual or infinitesimal progress rather than spectacular breakthroughs, and the rejection of a hypothesis after testing is still considered an advancement because it eliminates a hitherto untested hypothesis.

Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results kept as the work progressed? Although not explicitly stated in the text of the Income Tax Act or Regulations, contemporaneous record-keeping is implicit in the statutory requirement of a "systematic investigation". Furthermore, Justice Bowman emphasized that because section 37 is designed to encourage scientific research in Canada, it must receive a "fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as best ensures the attainment of its object" under section 12 of the Interpretation Act.

body.text: 8.2 Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 D.T.C. 1363, [1988] T.C.J. No. 409 (TCC)

In Sass Manufacturing, the taxpayer abandoned a failed pump development project and discarded its experimental records. Dismissing the appeal, Judge Sarchuk formulated the classic judicial definition of "systematic investigation" cited in the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors: "Systematic investigation connotes the existence of controlled experiments and of highly accurate measurements and involves the testing of one's theories against empirical evidence." Without controlled experiments and retained empirical measurements, shop-floor trial-and-error fails to qualify as SR&ED.
8.3 RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 99 D.T.C. 5087 (FCA)

In RIS-Christie (Docket A-710-96, decided December 21, 1998), the taxpayer invested in developing a cast-in-situ concrete forming spatial membrane, yielding a working prototype and a granted Canadian patent. Although the Tax Court judge accepted that testing occurred, a new product was created, and a technological advancement was achieved, the Tax Court dismissed the appeal because the taxpayer failed to produce detailed test records enabling third-party replication ("the repeatability criterion") after the lead engineer passed away. Speaking for a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal, Justice Robertson allowed the taxpayer's appeal with costs, holding that while documentary evidence is the "only sure-fire way" to prove systematic research, the Tax Court erred in law by treating documentary third-party repeatability as an absolute bar where established findings of fact already proved that testing occurred and produced a technological advancement. Justice Robertson distinguished Sass Manufacturing (where the project was abandoned and no advancement occurred) and confirmed that factual failure does not invalidate SR&ED, and that credible oral (viva voce) testimony can establish systematic investigation when supported by the totality of the evidence (as also illustrated in 116736 Ontario Ltd., Dockets 96-2484-IT and 96-4372-IT, where records were destroyed in a fire).
8.4 C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, [2002] 1 C.T.C. 212, 2002 D.T.C. 6740 (FCA)

In C.W. Agencies (Docket A-601-00, decided December 11, 2001), the Federal Court of Appeal affirmed Judge Bonner's disallowance of software SR&ED claims for a multilingual telephone/computer lottery ticket system and formally cemented the five-question Northwest Hydraulic test as the governing appellate standard across Canada. The jurisprudence also endorsed Judge Bonner's strict definition of a "hypothesis" as "a provisional concept which is not inconsistent with known facts and serves as a starting point for further investigation by which it may be proved or disproved objectively. In other words, a hypothesis is a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial."
8.5 Modern Appellate and Tax Court Jurisprudence (2011–2026)

Subsequent decisions have rigorously enforced every limb of the Northwest Hydraulic framework. In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen , 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355, the courts confirmed that solving technical problems through routine engineering or standard practice does not qualify. In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (TCC, January 2017, Docket 2015-125), Justice Sommerfeldt disallowed SR&ED claims where "Experiment Summary Sheets" had been prepared retroactively by an outside tax consultant long after the work concluded rather than contemporaneously. In Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen , 2017 TCC 205, the Tax Court underscored that all five Northwest Hydraulic questions must be answered in the affirmative, while Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen , 2017 TCC 42 illustrated how systematic hypothesis testing on pipe repair resins satisfies the test.

Finally, in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada , 2021 FCA 88 and National R&D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen , 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47) (and reiterated in Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada , 2026 FCA 175), the Federal Court of Appeal rejected taxpayer arguments that the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion (the "scientific method") lacked a statutory foundation in subsection 248(1) or had been superseded by the CRA's August 2021 Guidelines. Justice Rennie held that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the binding legal interpretation of subsection 248(1), that CRA administrative commentary does not bind the courts, and that the CRA's "How" requirement still requires underlying experimental rigour and discipline. Moreover, National R&D established strict appellate precedent on expert witness admissibility in Tax Court SR&ED appeals: the TCC and FCA excluded the taxpayer's proposed expert witness because the taxpayer's president had written 65% of the expert's report (violating impartiality and independence under the TCC Rules and Experts' Code of Conduct) and because the report impermissibly offered a legal opinion on whether the project met subsection 248(1).
9. Strategic Compliance Checklist for Canadian R&D Claimants
To maximize refundable cash recovery and maintain audit-ready compliance under the 2025–2026 Canadian SR&ED regime, claimants should implement the following eight-step operational protocol:

items: Apply for Optional Pre-Claim Approval (Form T1322) Prior to Project Launch: Submit Form T1322 through My Business Account before starting major R&D projects to secure a formal CRA eligibility determination (typically within 8 weeks, valid for up to 3 years), and enter the resulting case number on Lines 212 and 214 of Form T661 Version 26.

Evaluate the CCPC Revenue Election (Subsections 127(10.31) & (10.32)) and ECPC Qualification: Where a CCPC's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15 million, model the 3-year average annual revenue election under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) to preserve the $6,000,000 expenditure limit and $2,100,000 refundable 35% ITC, and verify ECPC consolidated group eligibility under subsections 127(9) and 127(10.6)–(10.62).

Compensate Specified Employees via Regular Payroll and File Form T1174: Pay founder-shareholders (>=10% share ownership) and non-arm's length family members through regular periodic salary rather than dividends or bonuses (which are disallowed under subsection 37(9)), file Form T1174 to allocate the 5 × YMPE cap ($356,500 in 2025; $373,000 in 2026) across associated corporations, and pay all accrued wages and current SR&ED expenses within 180 days of fiscal year-end.

Maintain Equipment-Use Logs for Restored Capital Property, SUE, and Leases (Post-December 15, 2024): Contemporaneously log equipment operating hours to substantiate >=90% ASA usage for capital equipment (Line 390 and Lines 262–263) and leased equipment (Line 350), or >50% to <90% primary usage for First and Second Term Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504) and Proxy Method half-lease claims (Line 355).

Tag Cloud Computing Environments and Structure Canadian Subcontracts: Use AWS/Azure/GCP resource tags to isolate experimental R&D compute from commercial COGS. Ensure arm's-length contracts are performed in Canada by taxable suppliers with clear statements of work and IP ownership, and execute Form T1146 for non-arm's length SR&ED transfers.

Optimize Multi-Program Stacking (NRC IRAP + Provincial Credits): Pair NRC IRAP salary grants with the Proxy Method so that the gross SR&ED salary base continues to generate the full 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount, and transition Quebec filings for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 to the new CRIC (Form RD-1029.8.CR) to capture both R&D and pre-commercialization expenses.

Embed Contemporaneous Evidence Collection into Engineering Workflows: Record technological uncertainties, testable hypotheses, experimental trials, failed iterations, and logical conclusions contemporaneously as the work progresses (Git commits, Jira tickets, architecture decision records, lab notebooks, and test logs) rather than reconstructing narratives after year-end.

Enforce the 18-Month Statutory Filing Calendar and Part 9 Disclosure: Calendar the absolute 18-month corporate deadline for filing both Form T661 (Version 26, including the Line 207 CRDC code) and Schedule T2SCH31, alongside provincial deadlines (such as Alberta AT1 Schedule 29 and Investissement Québec CDAE certifications), and verify complete Part 9 claim preparer disclosure to prevent subsection 37(12) forfeiture and subsection 162(5.1) $1,000 penalties.
